Kernel methods are commonly used in machine learning applications, though they suffer from significant computational costs for large datasets. This research introduces an innovative strategy to efficiently process large datasets. Traditionally, kernel methods rely on pre-computed kernel matrices, which can be time-consuming to calculate for extensive data sets. Our approach leverages random Fourier features to estimate the kernel function, eliminating the need for explicit computation. We enhance this method by developing a data-dependent variant of the random Fourier features' kernel estimation, which optimizes feature dimension based on the target model's sensitivity to noise. We thoroughly test and compare our approach against existing methods, demonstrating significant performance gains and robustness to noise.

This study investigates the notion of defining groups through polynomial equations, specifically focusing on how groups are established within the context of a given set of polynomials, known as Garland products. We examine the parameters that determine these products and identify a specific class of products that are effective in defining finite groups. Furthermore, we introduce a new decomposition approach called the Cartesian decomposition method, which enables us to generate effective Garland products for defining certain groups, including the Weyl group associated with the Lie algebra E8.

This research paper confirms that under a specific conformally smooth scenario, a particular type of geometric property known as M\"obius symmetry cannot be maintained for hypersurfaces within a hypersphere of higher dimensions, beyond the lowest dimension of three.

A new method of efficient wireless communication systems is proposed in a new research format, where data and energy are transmitted through separate frequency bands and power is harvested from the signal received. To analyze this system, a mathematical model with random variables representing received signal power and noise is developed. Expressions for the capacity of wireless communication systems and the energy harvested are derived from this model. It is discovered that there is an optimal distribution of time and frequency allocation to maximize the energy harvested and capacity of the wireless communication system respectively. A comparison with a traditional harvesting method shows that this new format can harvest more energy under certain conditions. A real-world implementation of this system is also outlined.

The Cayley graph of a random matrix algebra exhibits surprisingly complex behavior under avalanche scaling, despite these graphs typically being straightforward geometric representations. By analyzing the Cayley graph's random fluctuations and comparing it to the metric tree, we obtained a clear understanding of its asymptotic structure in the context of avalanche scaling. This structure is characterized by a set of conditions that define the graph's overall structure and determine which edges exist or disappear as the algebra's dimensions change. Our findings also reveal that the size of the graph's random fluctuations grow or decline at different rates, leading to distinct categories of behavior. Moreover, we found that many matrix algebras exhibit unique features that set them apart from random matrix algebras, which can be detected by studying the algebra's asymptotic distribution.

The detection of gravitational waves at high frequencies is limited by the backscatter of light on the photodetector, which causes signal delay and distortion. To overcome this constraint, we propose a novel device called the sloshing Sagnac interferometer, which uses a floating photodetector within an unloaded optical cavity to reduce light backscatter to nearly zero. By utilizing a loxodromic configuration and implementing a floating photodetector, we illustrate the potential for this sensor system to surpass the performance of traditional optical interferometers for gravitational wave detection at high frequencies.

This research examines a stochastic XL-MIMO network protocol to determine the optimal cell size. When MIMO bases are randomly generated and cells have no overlap, the research analyzes two area scenarios - one with rectangular bases and the other with non-circular, randomly shaped bases. For both scenarios, it is proven that there is a positive probability that, in a given area, no two cells have overlapping visibility areas. This probability is directly influenced by the area's size and shape, as well as the minimum distance between cells. It is also found that, in the limit as the number of users in each cell tends to infinity, the optimal cell size can be found by taking the derivative of the area function, which represents the total visible area in each cell. This derivative represents the rate at which the visible area in each cell changes when the system scales by a factor of one. Above this optimal size, the visible area in each cell decreases as the system scales, while below it, the visible area in each cell increases as the system scales. The research further examines the MIMO base distribution's impact on cell size by comparing two distributions - one concentrated on the center and the other more evenly distributed - and finds that the optimal cell size is directly influenced by the maximum base size. Recent observations at sub-millimeter/millimeter wavelengths have revealed that the morphological structure of young stars' surrounding disks comprise various shapes, including symmetrical patterns and features resembling spiral arms, and localized curved formations. Prior research primarily focused on modeling planetary interactions to explain observed patterns in disks. Although some exoplanets have been identified in such systems, many of these substructures emerge even before planetary formation as necessary precursors that lead to the creation of small solid particles, and ultimately, planetesimals. This work employs high-resolution, three-dimensional radiative hydrodynamic simulations that model the gas and solid particle interactions in protoplanetary disks. It highlights the distribution of small solid particles, formed through the vertical shear instability, and suggests that their characteristics align with features observed in recent sub-mm/mm wavelength observations. It also predicts future observable signatures in the electromagnetic spectrum from the particles, which may be found in specific spectral bands, such as the $890\mu m$ band, and suggest strategies for identifying these markers in ongoing and future surveys.

Researchers used the Relativistic Mean Field model to study the properties of a neutron star formed from isospin symmetry breaking, assuming the neutron-star matter includes hyperon matter and magnetic matter. By comparing the neutron-star mass and radius in various models and with or without isospin breaking, a minimum allowed radius of approximately 27.4 km was determined for neutron stars with masses between 0.5 to 2.6 solar masses. This radius holds across different models and variations of isospin breaking. Isospin breaking causes the neutron star to have a maximum allowed mass of 2.69 solar masses and affects the magnetic field strength and the neutral kaon condensation phase transition.

This research focuses on creating the molecular S{\o}rensen gate in multiple motional modes, ensuring the accuracy of frequency measurements and expanding the gate's tolerance to frequency shifts caused by dephasing. A proposed implementation using two-dimensional pseudospectroscopy is analyzed, with simulations demonstrating successful execution of the S{\o}rensen gate across various scenario combinations. A key finding reveals that using a beam splitting device to create coherent states results in a balanced superposition, which is crucial for achieving high precision in frequency measurements. Additionally, our results show that the magnitude of frequency shifts during dephasing has a significant impact on the gate's success rate, with recommended experimental parameters including a difference in carrier frequencies of at least half the motional frequency to prevent significant shifts during dephasing.

Lately, researchers have focused intensely on misfit cobalt oxide layers, particularly $B$_2CO$_3$ on Si(001), which exhibit unique properties resulting from their interplay of covalent in-plane and weak out-of-plane bonds. By developing an sp$^2$-hybridization-inspired model, we have delved deeper into the theoretical foundations of these materials. Our proposed model includes a specific crystal structure prediction for a particular layer in relation to its substrate, which agrees with experimental data. Furthermore, using a tight-binding Hamiltonian approach, we were able to replicate and explain existing experimental results on the material's energy spectra and optical properties. Our model predicts the materials' energy spectra to remain essentially unchanged along the $\Gamma$-X direction due to their two-dimensional (2D) character. Moreover, we expect a significant increase in the direct bandgap size under strain, which could be achieved by heating the silicon substrate. These predictions indicate that these materials could possess a unique property called the "Dirac cone damping," where a particular energy spectrum feature remains undamaged, even when the materials' dimension transitions from 2D to three-dimensional (3D). This phenomenon occurs because of the materials' large and anisotropic effective mass in the 3D state. As a result, we expect these materials to exhibit exceptional optical properties in both their 2D and 3D states, which could be controlled by strain induced by heating the substrate.

The NA62 experiment at CERN's 50 GeV proton beam facility can detect rare decay events of positive kaons. With its highly efficient rejection of background processes, the experiment can utilize a specialized setup for decay observations. By utilizing the current setup, NA62 can enhance sensitivity for a specific neutral lepton scenario where a neutrally charged particle is generated in the decay process $K^+ \to \pi^0 e^+ N$. By calculating detection probabilities, the experiment can place constraints on neutral lepton properties such as its mass and coupling strength. Calculations indicate that for a neutrally charged particle with a mass below 200 MeV, the NA62 experiment can place a coupling strength limit below $2.5 \times 10^{-16}$, surpassing existing constraints by a factor of 5. Additionally, the detector can also place constraints on rare decay processes like $K^+ \to e^+ \gamma N$ and $K^+ \to \mu^+ \gamma N$.

Neural language models have largely surpassed $N$-gram models due to better performance, but our findings suggest that $n$-gram models still excel in many situations with low computational costs, demonstrating a strong foundation of linguistic knowledge. Building upon this discovery, we developed a neural language model through residual learning, incorporating the strengths of both models. By pretraining a neural language model on $n$-gram-based pseudo-data, we achieved significant improvements in various evaluation metrics. Notably, our approach led to notable gains in low-data-setting situations and demonstrated versatility in incorporating external knowledge easily. Evaluations with human assessors also indicated a perceived increase in coherence and overall quality of the generated text.

Reconstructing three-dimensional faces from single two-dimensional images is a complex task due to varying lighting conditions, facial occlusions, and image degradation. This process can be broken down into identifying important pixels that contain facial features and constructing a three-dimensional face model based on these pixels. A new framework called SADRNet addresses both of these challenging aspects by incorporating a prior understanding of face structures and utilizing a self-correcting mechanism to enhance the accuracy of reconstructed models. The proposed network consists of multiple stages that work in conjunction to refine the reconstruction process, and it demonstrates significant improvements over existing methods in terms of both quantitative and qualitative performance measures, particularly in scenarios with partially obscured faces.

Within the framework of the $\alpha$-attractor inflation model, we undertake a comprehensive perturbative approach to examine the role of cosmological perturbations in identifying primordial black holes. Our investigation focuses on a specific aspect of perturbations - scalar metric perturbations - in order to determine the mass fraction of black holes formed during the early universe. We achieved this by correlating the density of perturbations with the mass of black holes, utilizing a criterion based on the boundary condition at the end of inflation. Our results reveal that the mass of black holes is proportional to the amplitude of perturbations squared, also found to be in proportion to the overall density of matter. Consequently, we found that the mass fraction of black holes can be determined by integrating over the mass fraction formed during each-kernel region, with a condition that the perturbations within these kernels exceed a threshold that determines formation requirements. Our analysis further shows that the relation between the mass fraction of black holes and the overall density of matter can be accurately represented by a second-order polynomial, with results specifically applicable to a range of spectral indices from 10^-10 up to 10^-2. Additionally, we derived an alternative, more straightforward method of determining the mass fraction of black holes, bypassing our previous perturbative analysis, with results demonstrating similarities to the earlier outcomes.

Consider an ordered tree with labeled nodes. If we arrange the nodes in ascending order, some of the node labels will be equal, indicating multiple occurrences of the same vertex. Our task is to identify the number of these distinct vertices, taking into account the tree's structure and the differences between its nodes. In this study, we establish that in a tree of size $n$, the number of deepest vertices can be anywhere from $1$ to $\left\lfloor\frac{n}{\lfloor\log_2 n\rfloor}\rfloor$; furthermore, we prove that there are trees of any given size that have exactly $k$ deepest vertices for all possible values of $k$ within this range.

This research focuses on the manual process of counting votes through mark-filled ballots, a step that involves converting scanned images of these ballots into accurate numerical data. To achieve this, Informed Optical Character Recognition (iOCR) technology was developed, a specialized version of OCR tailored to ballot counts. This system leverages a pre-existing algorithm to identify areas of the scanned images containing numbers, before using a more sophisticated character recognition algorithm to convert these identified areas into numerical data. In tests using large datasets from Australian state elections, iOCR was found to outperform standard OCR technology by significant margins, with an overall accuracy rate of 94% for Australian State Election Ballots.

In recent developments of large-scale linear models, researchers have discovered that, counterintuitively, models with overparameterization can still obtain exact solutions and efficient training by employing optimization algorithms like stochastic gradient descent. This phenomenon is observed regardless of data characteristics, including whether data is linearly independent. This study extends the overparameterization framework to include time series data with dependencies and finds that GD-based optimization algorithms can lead to highly accurate results, even when data exhibits strong temporal correlations. A statistical theory is developed to ensure that these algorithms converge to accurate solutions within a single iteration, and our results are demonstrated through simulated and real-world examples of time series data.

Fluctuations in energy demand lead to varying market prices for electricity, affecting profitability when storing large amounts of electricity in massive facilities.  As a result, there has been an increasing interest in optimizing the sizing of these storage systems across various contexts. While existing methods typically focus on utilizing optimistic future price forecasts, this research explores the benefits of incorporating uncertainty in price forecasts, thereby influencing storage sizing decisions. We develop a decision-making framework that accounts for the sensitivity of storage sizing to future prices, effectively making "cautious" decisions. This approach is particularly useful when future prices have complex, interdependent patterns. We apply this method to realistic test cases based on actual electricity price data. Our results show that failing to consider the effects of price forecasting on storage sizing can result in incorrect decisions, ultimately leading to suboptimal results.

A simplified computer model has been compared to another similar model to analyze how atmospheric circulation behaves in extremely rotating planets. Despite significant differences in size and mass, the two models exhibit comparable circulation patterns, suggesting they behave in a similar way. The models show that in very fast-rotating planets with thin atmospheres, circulation is controlled by the speed of sound rather than the Earth-like reference frame. This result explains earlier observations of unusual atmospheric behavior in these types of planets. Additionally, the models reveal that the movement of atmospheric particles becomes more random as the speed of rotation increases, influencing the formation of large circulation patterns.

The recent rise of large language models has led to significant progress in multiple tasks, demonstrating the benefit of transfer learning. Nonetheless, the extent to which these models can be effectively trained on a dynamic schedule has not been thoroughly explored. Our investigation focuses on determining whether fully pre-trained language models can be efficiently fine-tuned on a subset of the ImageNet dataset through the cosine decay learning schedule, without benefitting from additional data. Surprisingly, our findings reveal that many commonly used models perform remarkably well without further training, surpassing the performance of traditional learning strategies for certain tasks. Moreover, we observe that certain models exhibit robust performance across numerous classification problems, suggesting they can be a valuable starting point for various future endeavors.

Researchers who implement quantum computing for simulating chemical processes via CI methods can utilize effective weight theories to streamline efforts. This approach eliminates the need to manage vast amounts of orbital data while maintaining accuracy in results. The study demonstrates the effectiveness of this method by applying multi-valley effective weight theory to exchange-linked donor processes in silicon, accounting for valley and spin interactions. The resulting simulations yield reliable results for donor pairs across different energy regimes, even without incorporating orbital details. The research showcases the promise of this efficient method for addressing complex systems and donor coupled systems beyond the reach of actual quantum devices but relevant to upcoming experimental implementations.

Our investigation focused on theoretical analyses of quantum trenches made from HgTe material, which exhibit unique properties due to a lack of a bandgap. Utilizing the Dirac-Schrödinger model, we were able to study these structures under different levels of complexity. Initially, we examined a simple quantum well with a gapless energy spectrum, and then proceeded to more complex designs, including antiferromagnetic ordering and doped state, where we identified localized states within the quantum trenches. Throughout our study, we prioritized accuracy in our results by employing a bulk Hamiltonian parameterization method, which allowed us to utilize established knowledge of Kramers-theorem-based energy spectra in simple models. Our findings were then compared to actual experiments conducted on HgTe quantum wells.

In Dynamic Time-Division Duplexing (TDD), model allocation refers to determining when different TDD configurations should be used based on varying channel conditions and network requirements. This process needs to be highly dynamic to adapt to mobile devices moving quickly. However, traditional TDD model allocation methods, which utilize static models and inflexible configurations, may struggle to perform well in such environments. In contrast, we propose a novel approach that utilizes machine learning and dynamic TDD models to maximize the efficiency of network resources. Specifically, we use a payoff function to evaluate the effectiveness of different TDD models and apply an evolutionary algorithm to determine the optimal allocation. When implemented in a 5G network, our method demonstrates a significant increase in network throughput and capacity, especially in areas with low TDD bandwidth. Additionally, our method can adapt to changes in the environment within just a few seconds.

In this work, we investigate the capacity of Hamiltonian Neural Networks with quadratic potentials to accurately replicate gradient computations. Through a series of experiments involving stochastic optimization on various models, we find that HNNs are capable of replicating gradient calculations and, as a result, can be utilized for dynamic regularization techniques like gradient descent with damping. Furthermore, we observe that HNNs can emulate the effects of learning rate schedules and adaptive optimization methods. The conditions under which HNNs fail to accurately replicate certain gradients, particularly those associated with non-Euclidean norms, also become apparent from our experiments. The code used in this research has been made publicly available.

AI models can sometimes reject valid data, causing problems with training. To address this issue, a method was proposed to improve the quality of machine learning models by allowing them to interact with humans. In this interaction, human judges provide classifications for unknown samples, which are then used to correct their models. The approach uses optimization to minimize both model error and the rejection of new data. This results in a system of differential equations that can be solved through numerical methods. The proposed method was tested on several datasets with varying levels of purity, showing improvements in model performance and a decrease in rejected data.

We create a scalar invariant for specific types of linked knots in a twisted tube format, identified by a pair of tori linked via two Klein bottles and eight twisted tubes. This construction draws from the work of Dunhelewicz, Garshelis, and Kania, who established an analogous invariant for links in the product of two tori. Our newly developed invariant demonstrates that the sum of its absolute values, in relation to a specific scaling factor, remains constant for a particular class of twisted tubes with volume hypothesis behavior.

The primary objective of Word Sense Disambiguation (WSD) involves determining the appropriate sense of a word with multiple meanings within a particular context.  Advances in deep learning, specifically utilizing BERT, have led to significant progress in this area, with several strategies employed to combine context and gloss information to achieve this goal.  Based on existing research using BERT, a novel method is proposed that incorporates a gloss-enhancement context to build on the fundamental idea of combining context and gloss information.  Experimental results using the SenseVal framework demonstrate improved performance for 9 out of 12 tested datasets, with an average increase in accuracy of 2.5%.  The proposed approach is also highly effective in difficult WSD instances, as identified by human annotators, with a 25% increase in accuracy.

This study provides a set of transformed Gamma function integrals that the authors have derived in a previous work, with the additional transformation of changing the function's reciprocity. Similar to the original results, these formulas maintain the same convergence properties of their underlying components and are intended for the purpose of consolidating the Gamma function's definition through its integral representations, despite the fact that these formulations are more complex than the standard or reciprocal versions.

The potential for deep learning approaches to employ generation-specific characteristics to identify quarks in proton-nucleus collisions is considered. By utilizing a dataset of simulated proton-proton collisions, a convolutional neural network was trained to distinguish between top quarks produced via the sub-processes $pp \to tt$ and $pp \to Wb$ at the LHC. The model's performance under realistic detection conditions was evaluated using a detector simulation for the ALICE experiment. The study indicates that, with appropriate reconstruction techniques, there is a practical opportunity to differentiate between the two quark generations via statistical analyses of correlated particle distributions. The study also provides initial estimates of the expected accuracy of quark generation identification at the LHC energy regime for the ALICE experiment.

This study focuses on transferring SQL databases generated from real-world data, such as Yelp, across domains. To achieve this, we propose a two-part approach: first, we develop a method to automatically create simple SQL databases from a given text dataset; second, we design a supporting task to refine the generated databases. In both stages, we employ a seamless, end-to-end framework called "TextIL" without requiring manual specification of columns or custom templates. Our experiments demonstrate that both methods successfully enhance the accuracy of generated databases. Specifically, we find that Yale Yale, a Yale-based database generated from Yale text, exhibits superior performance compared to a straight transfer from the original Yale database. Our proposed framework and supporting task achieve CMR scores of 22.5 and 34.6 on the Yale dataset, respectively. Additionally, our results reveal that using Yale Yale as a bridge successfully transfers databases to new domains, yielding a 6.1% CMR score improvement over a straight transfer.

Modern organizations rely heavily on graph-based platforms to manage and analyze complex data, incorporating numerous attributes and relationships. As a result of this diversity, sensitive information is frequently incorporated into these graphs, posing a significant threat of unauthorized disclosure. To address this issue, researchers have developed a variety of methods to ensure the confidentiality of graph-organized data, leading to a proliferation of techniques and models. However, these methods often overlap, making it difficult to gain a unified understanding. In response to these challenges, we have crafted a comprehensive survey that categorizes existing techniques into four disciplines: classification, optimization, machine learning, and smart contracts. Within each category, we delve into specific algorithms and evaluate their performance through thorough simulations. Our study is designed to serve as a foundation for further innovative work in differential confidentiality for graph-organized data.

The vast amount of images Euclid will produce during its operation, exceeding 70 million high-quality images per day, poses both a challenge and opportunity for its telescope and mission design. To meet the demands of rapid image capture, the camera systems will operate at a pace that requires developing heritage technology to a high degree. As a result, Euclid will leverage existing technology effectively and build upon it, rather than adopting entirely new concepts. This document outlines the potential for heritage science in Euclid, with a focus on identifying areas where developed technology can be refined to meet the camera's needs. It also explores opportunities for further scientific applications of this heritage technology across various fields, including astronomy, medicine, geology, and cultural heritage conservation, among others.

Researchers have developed a quantum hydrodynamic framework, expressed in Wigner functions and operator-valued distributions, to describe complex Bose systems driven by interactions and quantum fluctuations. This approach has led to novel insights into hydrodynamic theory at the quantum level and has facilitated a nonlinear quantum hydrodynamic model. The model's predictions have been validated through comparisons with numerical data from mean-field theories, and its scope has been expanded to encompass non-equilibrium situations by introducing a quantum hydrodynamic model with noise. This model's capabilities in capturing both noisy stationary states and dynamic processes are demonstrated. The developed framework offers a versatile tool for investigating interacting Bose systems and provides a theoretical context for understanding the noise effects on hydrodynamic theory at the quantum level.

Given an alphabet $\mathcal{A}$ and a sequence $\mathcal{F}_n$ of $n$-variant stochastic processes defined on $\mathcal{A}$, we prove that for processes with which which induce a total variation distance to independence that scales at a rate greater than $1/\sqrt{n}$, the total variation distance to independence is detectable using $n$ sample paths from $\mathcal{F}_n$. Similarly, for an alphabet $\mathcal{A}$ with $|\mathcal{A}| = K$ and a sequence $\mathcal{F}_n$ of $n$-variant stochastic processes defined on $\mathcal{A}$, we show that the total variation distance to independence is detectable using $nK$ sample paths from $\mathcal{F}_n$ provided that the rate scaling is greater than $1/\sqrt{nK}$. These results extend the deviation principles initially established by Choudhuri, Venkatasubramanian, and Walkery and later extended by Birkner, Greven, and Hoffman to independent identically distributed random variables to independent identically distributed stochastic processes.

Given a metric space that contains two distinct points, we can define a homotopy class as the set of paths between these points that can be continuously deformed.  Within the context of a specific type of metric space called an inverse complete vector space, we can identify areas that minimize homotopy classes of closed curves.  These areas satisfy a property related to the minimum of a surface with respect to a specific energy functional, and they are also connected to the concept of minimal surfaces with boundary characteristics similar to those of a sphere with two holes.  Additionally, we can define areas that minimize homotopy classes of curves with no self-intersections, and these areas are linked to the energy functional of a surface with characteristics similar to those of a torus with one hole.  These relationships remain valid even when the metric space includes additional points, as long as it remains an inverse complete vector space.  Furthermore, we can extend these results to areas that minimize homotopy classes of curves with up to three self-intersections, as well as areas that minimize homotopy classes of a curve with an arbitrary number of self-intersections, provided that the metric space has a specific topological characteristic and is an inverse complete vector space.

Understanding how the strong interaction chooses between different forms of a nucleus isn't fully comprehended. Research indicates that both Coulomb excitation and alpha-cluster interaction are significant in forming 64Ni, which is peculiar since nickel generally resists alpha-clusters. A recent study employs the monopole tensor interaction within the GDR energy distribution to study the structure of 64Ni. By comparing energy shifts and widths, researchers found that the tensor interaction favors a specific collective motion in 64Ni. Additionally, combining experimental data with theoretical predictions points to a small likelihood of null spin parity occurrence in 64Ni. Further investigation is needed to completely unravel the structure of 64Ni.

Machine learning models, including NLP models, often suffer from two significant issues when validating and tuning: overfitting and variance. While techniques such as k-fold cross validation address overfitting by reducing model size and complexity, they can lead to inflated estimates of performance due to variance, particularly when tuning is done with limited data. This paper advises using the j-k fold cross validation method to address this issue, as it involves conducting k iterations of cross validation to determine the optimal model size and complexity, and then selecting the results from the j largest and smallest sets of cross validation scores to reduce variance and overfitting. This approach is straightforward to implement and does not incur significant computational costs, making it a practical solution for tackling real-world problems like NLP.

Intelligent agents, including those learning through instruction, have traditionally been viewed as equal partners in knowledge sharing. This partnership perspective, reflected in identical structures for both parties, has been the basis for various learning model designs. However, this review suggests that such a symmetric approach may not always be the most suitable option for modeling learning processes. By examining various learning dynamics, including those involving instruction and those that are self-driven, this review finds that a asymmetric structure, characterized by distinct forms for agents with different levels of expertise, can often yield more effective results. Consequently, this review advocates for a more flexible approach to learning model design, one that incorporates an asymmetric structure to accommodate diverse learning scenarios.

Given a binary graphical model, determining the most probable explanation (MPE) is a fundamental task with various applications, including solving systems of inequalities, identifying maximal independent sets, and resolving boolean optimization problems. Although several fast approximate methods for MPE exist, there's also a significant interest in exact algorithms like the Universal Categorization Algorithm. However, even though this method achieves optimal results, its high computational cost makes it unsuitable for large-scale systems. Our novel technique, the Binary Function Categorization method, leverages a different approach to tackle large models. By dividing the possible function values into categorized groups based on the maximum value and the difference between values, this method prevents unnecessary categorization that increases computation. Furthermore, our algorithm avoids creating a large number of small categories that provide no useful information, thereby enhancing efficiency. The Binary Function Categorization method enables the fast execution of both limited optimization and exact MPE, outperforming existing exact methods and surpassing the performance of many faster approximate methods.

We investigated the effects of a returning photon from absorption spectroscopy on strontium atoms with excess kinetic energy, and how this might influence the development of sensitive and precise frequency measurements. By employing theoretical models and ultra-cold strontium atoms, our research revealed that even with very sensitive detection methods, the absorption signals remain essentially unchanged, due to the scattered photons being shifted out of the measured signal range. Furthermore, this leads to a finding that the motivation for considering the influence of recoil effects is mitigated. Consequently, we found that with a very narrow laser, the main constraint on accuracy is caused by the motion of the atoms, rather than the recurrence of photons, and is determined by a trade-off between reducing atomic motion through cooling and widening the laser's frequency range, which affects the measurement's sensitivity and ability to detect a signal.

For periodic shear flows subject to a destabilizing force, such as Coriolis or shear-driven instability, this research reveals that the point of transition is proportionally affected by the size of the system, including both its length and width, and this scaling holds true for the onset of both secondary and tertiary shear-driven instability.

Recently introduced is a class of algebras known as Racah algebras, which stem from the stabilizer of the Coxeter group $\mathfrak{S}_4$ and contain the $\mathfrak{sl}_2$ Lie algebra as a Lie subalgebra. This report delves into specific aspects of these algebras, specifically the enumerative properties associated with them. It is demonstrated that the stabilizer $Z_n(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$, defined as the fixed points of $\mathfrak{sl}_2$ acting by scalar multiplication on the algebra with a specific structure, exhibits Hecke algebra properties when $n$ is an odd number. Furthermore, it is shown that $Z_3(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ is equivalent to the Askey-Wilson algebra, a result that can be viewed as a combinatorial interpretation of this algebra's defining relations.

An important aspect of Web search optimization involves making adjustments to search engine results pages (SERPs) to better match a user's expectations. Although this customization can lead to higher satisfaction ratings and repeated business, it's likely to have a negative side effect: pertinent information outside of preferred results may go unnoticed. If this phenomenon has significant consequences, it could contribute substantially to the overlooking of vital information, which may even have severe implications for critical decisions. To investigate this hypothesis, a relevant butSupplementary Web page was created to serve as a control page for a study on the perception of Web search customization. The study's aim was to examine the phenomenon described in this paper through a controlled experiment. Participants were directed to one of two pages containing 30 Web search results each for the term "what causes cancer." The only difference between the directed pages was the presence or absence of customized SERPs. The customized page was obtained using Google's regular search results. The main focus of the study was on one of the 30 results, number 10. It was hypothesized that users directed to the customized page would be less likely to notice result number 10 from the search results than those directed to the regular search results. To validate this hypothesis, the customized and regular search pages were re-created with new queries. The results from both experiments showed that users directed to the customized page were significantly less likely to notice result number 10 from the search results than those directed to the regular search results. We are suggesting the construction of a muon particle accelerator that uses a collider to study matter formed in the early universe. This facility would allow for the examination of neutrino properties and the study of a specific process called "muon capture," which involves an atomic nucleus absorbing a muon and neutrinos. We believe such a facility has vast potential for both theoretical and experimental physics advancements. We are proposing a design for the accelerator and collider that includes a 20 kilometer muon ring and multiple particle rings with different sizes, capable of operating at various energies. We estimate the total construction cost to be approximately 10 billion dollars. This project could be realized through public and private funding and would require approximately 10 years to complete. We are also exploring alternative designs for a smaller-scale facility that could be constructed more quickly and cheaply.

The current 4D T2-weighted images are acquired over several minutes, which may limit their effectiveness for rapid diagnostic assessments. This study demonstrates the feasibility of a novel technique to achieve high-quality 4D T2-weighted images in as little as two minutes through rapid breathing cycles, eliminating the need for continuous scanning. By leveraging a combination of techniques including motion estimation, model-based reconstruction, and variable density sampling, the proposed method delivers 4D T2-weighted images after post-processing, which show comparable performance to traditional 4D T2-weighted images obtained through continuous scanning. The proposed method has been effectively implemented and tested on a 1.5T MRI scanner for rapid 4D T2-weighted imaging of abdominal cavities, yielding promising early results.

The paired-permutation test metric has been effective in guiding the sampling process in structured prediction tasks, demonstrating precise performance in NLP applications. However, the method's sensitivity to a perfect pairing of predicted and actual outcomes can pose a challenge, especially in scenarios with significantly imbalanced data. To address this issue, we propose a variant of the paired-permutation method, designed to accommodate datasets with a high degree of structural complexity. Unlike the standard paired-permutation approach, our method considers the potential disintegration of paired relationships under permutation. As such, we refer to it as the paired-permutation method's generalization, specifically the precise paired-permutation examination (PPEX). Evaluations of PPEX on tasks including the CONVENE game, span reconstruction, and machine translation have shown its capacity to surpass the performance of the standard paired-permutation method across various metrics. Moreover, PPEX demonstrates the ability to surpass the performance of the standard paired-permutation method at a relatively fast sampling rate, indicating its potential for broad applicability in NLP.

A comprehensive dataset of freight costs, shipping volumes, new ship constructions, used ship sales, and scrap sales has been assembled from 1966 to 2009 for eight major routes and eight types of cargo ships. Furthermore, an analysis of recent industry developments and available historical data is presented. The dataset incorporates various variables that previous studies have found to influence freight costs, including fuel costs, new ship sales prices, used ship sales prices, and an index of global economic activity. Notably, the current dataset deviates from prior research by incorporating a plethora of new independent variables such as ship demolition values, time series spanning nearly five decades, that significantly expand the existing dataset of 12 observations for each ship type.

Inspired by the fabric theory of Conradian graphs, we develop a new mathematical framework called fabric spaces to investigate knotting and twisting phenomena. This approach is characterized by a specific type of periodic flow called hyperwiring, which generates graph models that reflect the complex structures of knot diagrams. As a result, we are able to apply statistical mechanics techniques to describe and study these models. In the process, our research yields a novel interpretation of Bacher, Seroussi, and Velu's helix gas model in terms of hyperwiring, which allows us to extend their results to a broader context. Additionally, our method enables us to explore new models, such as the helix fabric model, that exhibit an intriguing transition phase resulting from hyperwiring, which may be understood as a discrete version of the knotting transition.

The recent interest in the stock market can be attributed to growing inflation rates prompting people to invest in equities, commodities, and other assets, as opposed to saving. Deep-learning-based techniques are now the predominant approach for predicting stock prices. Our proposed framework combines two innovative concepts: Stock Price Forecasting using BERT and GAN. BERT is utilized for extracting relevant financial indicators from noisy data, thereby serving as the basis for our GAN-based forecast model. Additionally, we introduce two novel concepts: Inclusion of technical indicators derived from chart patterns to enhance forecasting accuracy and a strategy to prevent vanishing gradients during training. Our model demonstrates superior performance compared to existing methods across various metrics including the RMSE, MAE, and MAPE values of 0.541, 0.345, and 0.134, respectively, as evidenced by a significant increase in Sharpe ratio (from 2.51 to 10.81) and a decrease in Skewness (from -0.87 to -0.01) and Kurtosis (from 1.56 to 2.16).

This research investigates the production of two Higgs bosons at future electron-positron colliders with an energy of 1 TeV or more, facilitated through the interaction of Higgs with heavy top quarks within the framework of Effective Field Theories, beyond the standard model. We examine how this process is influenced by beyond-Standard Model Higgs interactions and identify which experiments can effectively measure this process at various Effective Field Theory scales, thereby providing meaningful constraints on beyond-Standard Model physics. Moreover, we analyze the sensitivity of these experiments to certain beyond-Standard Model operators, particularly those related to the interaction between a singlet scalar and either heavy top quarks or Higgs bosons. We also explore the potential for future lepton colliders to combine Higgs and top quark effective data, enabling a more comprehensive understanding of beyond-Standard Model physics.

We provide an analysis of the fundamental requirements for a gravitational theory to be consistent with general relativity. This involves examining the conditions under which the Poisson operator, a central component of Lagrangian density construction, yields a vanishing divergence when acting on vector fields, and we explore both explicit and implicit condition cases. A computational method for the implicit case is also presented.

We investigated the drag experienced by a long cylindrical solid moving through a layer of granular material filled with fluid, focusing on the differences in drag forces it encounters when moving in opposite directions. Our findings showed that this solid generally experiences a greater drag force when moved in one particular direction than the other, a phenomenon we call drag asymmetry. The magnitude of this asymmetry was observed to increase with a higher speed of movement and greater friction between the solid and the surrounding granular material. Furthermore, the point of 50% drag equality was found to occur at approximately 32 degrees of the angle of recoil, which is a key result that can be explained by a simple theoretical model.

Our recent calculations within the RHICMultiplicity Framework, which incorporates both radial flow and anisotropic flow from a hadronic transport model, yield triangular flow results that lie above existing data for Au+Au and Cu+Cu collisions. This excess is particularly pronounced at lower particle densities, where our model predicts $v_3/\epsilon_3$ values of 0.17 and 0.25 for mid-central Au+Au and Cu+Cu collisions, respectively. In contrast, our results show that $v_3/\epsilon_3$ increases with multiplicity in our model, the opposite of observed trends for $v_3/\epsilon_3$ in Au+Au and Cu+Cu collisions. Notably, our calculations also indicate that initial condition anisotropy $\epsilon_3$ decreases with increasing particle density, the opposite of the predicted behavior based on participant anisotropy alone. We argue that early moments of relativistic heavy-ion collisions may be more sensitive to initial state fluctuations than traditional flow measures, suggesting that higher-order anisotropic flows could serve as direct probes of local charge density fluctuations.

The study evaluates theoretical predictions for unusual processes involving beauty mesons, specifically those that involve unique polarizations and entangled quark and antiquark systems, which display CP non-conformity. The analysis considers both neutral and charged beauty mesons within the bottom and strange family. The calculation of unusual polarization patterns and rare decays that defy CP standards are examined in both neutral and charged beauty mesons. Unlike rare decays induced by electroweak interactions, these processes are influenced by the strong force and are therefore more accessible in experiments. The research focuses on unconventional decay pathways of beauty mesons that defy CP conventions, specifically via strange mesons to leptons, and evaluates the likelihood of these events at various particle accelerators. The research focuses on unconventional decay pathways of beauty mesrons that defy CP conventions, specifically via strange mesons to leptons, and evaluates the likelihood of these events at various particle accelerators.

A key characteristic of model reduction methods, particularly when applying them to morphable models, is the preservation of shape constraints. Despite the benefits, there are challenges in utilizing these methods in certain contexts due to their complex nature. This work presents a straightforward approach to creating efficient Krylov solvers that maintain stability and adhere to shape-preserving conditions, even in the presence of significant time steps or sparse matrices requiring iterative solution methods. A representative example involving acoustic wave propagation and shape-preserving reduction is provided.

We present a novel method for aligning non-rigid volumes with surface data, incorporating a biomechanical model that utilizes a finite element method to simulate tissue behavior, and we demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach for aligning volume and surface data.

Learning scene flow from monocular images poses a significant problem for machines due to the need for training data, making it an important task for artificial intelligence to be able've own learning capabilities. In order to overcome this obstacle, the researchers propose a novel approach called Adversarial Metric Learning for self-taught flow estimation, allowing the model to make use of geometric information derived from any image it is presented with, without relying on supervisory signals. The proposed method leverages an adversarial loss function in conjunction with a metric learning loss function to ensure that the model's predictions align with the image-derived geometry. Further enhancements to the approach are achieved by introducing an occlusion-aware loss function to address issues related to metric learning in complex and overlapping areas. The method is evaluated on a public dataset with rigorous experiments, demonstrating its superior performance in comparison to alternative self-supervised and supervised methods.

In recent years, Random Neural Networks (RNNs) have gained popularity due to their efficiency in pattern recognition tasks, despite the lack of a clear understanding of their internal workings. Based on the premise that categorization reflects the outcome of a comparison process, we've developed a revised version of a spiking RNN that produces superior results, with a novel output mechanism that produces a delay-based comparison effect. By incorporating a more advanced categorization mechanism, this version outperforms traditional RNNs in many situations. Our experiments show that this version excels in both accuracy and energy efficiency when classifying data, demonstrating significant improvements of 6.8% in accuracy and 5.8% in energy efficiency for a specific dataset.

This research investigates the thermodynamic characteristics of quark matter under high temperature and magnetic field conditions, specifically focusing on spin-aligned quark matter. The study assumes that quark matter consists of electrons, muons, and strange quarks in equal proportions. Using the MIT bag model, we derived the thermodynamic potential for spin-aligned quark matter and subsequently constructed the mean-field model. Consequently, we obtained the pressure-density relation for spin-aligned quark matter at finite temperature and magnetic field. This relation enabled us to determine the mass-radius relationships for spin-aligned strange quark stars across various conditions.

Every perfect matching in a cubic graph can be associated with a Hamiltonian cycle, whose vertices are determined by the pairs of edges in the graph's ideal pairing corresponding to the matching's components. We demonstrate that each rotation of the Hamiltonian cycle can be represented by a switch in the ideal pairing, which alters two edge pairs into two individual edges. By analyzing the changes to the pairing, we can identify the properties of a specific edge and its surrounding structure. Using these properties, we can identify all the edges surrounding a specific edge in a Hamiltonian cycle and thus retrieve the original Hamiltonian cycle. This process is equivalent to executing a sequence of edge switches, which can be seen as a form of edge mutation. We define a set of edge mutations that map one ideal pairing to another, and show that they satisfy the conditions of being consistent, closed under reversal, and generating all possible pairings. Notably, these mutations preserve the parity of the graph's Euler characteristic.

This paper introduces a new technique called Timeloops for automating the creation of system call filtering rules in containerized applications. During operation, Timeloops can automatically determine which system calls are made by each component of a system, based on historical usage data. It then combines these determinations into a set of efficient rules that can be used to enhance security and efficiency by limiting the scope of system call auditing. Our research used a simplified model to test the performance of Timeloops on small applications, but also successfully applied the method to real-world, complex containers, achieving a 10 times reduction in system call auditing output. Our findings are that a simple, empirical approach based on usage patterns can lead to a 20 times decrease in system call auditing results, and that Timeloops can also be used in scenarios where system call filtering is not necessary, providing a 10 times speedup in system call auditing. Our research into various profiling approaches revealed that, in order of effectiveness, there are static, hybrid, and dynamic methods of profiling containers, and concluded with an analysis of the potential vulnerabilities of system call filtering, and an overview of the implementation of Timeloops.

This study develops a Poisson multi-Bernoulli mixture (PMBM) filter where target appearance probabilities are organized around a lattice, rather than a global framework. This innovative approach excels in scenarios where the state space is considerable, offering a significant reduction in computation and storage requirements. A primary application of this advancement is in dynamic systems with moving sensors, particularly those with radial motion, where a circular lattice structure offers substantial performance gains.

This study examines the null controllability of a partial differential equation involving a degenerate population model with spatial distribution and migration aspects. By first establishing a new Carleman estimate for the adjoint system in its entirety, and subsequently deriving a relevant observability inequality, we aim to demonstrate the existence of a localized control mechanism capable of driving the population towards extinction within a finite time frame.

In soccer, a small number of key moments can decide the outcome of an otherwise even match.  Due to the limited data available for many teams, a new challenge arises in modeling these situations with machine learning.  Current methods require large datasets with detailed information about game progress, making them unsuitable for many cases.  In response, we propose a novel way to use reinforcement learning for better strategy in these critical moments.  By creating a controlled environment that mimics real games, we can use agents to test different team behavior, then use the results to train a model of the game.  By building a model of the game instead of relying on data, this approach can handle any team in any situation, without the need for pre-existing data.  To validate our method, we compare the performance of a standard agent in a simulated game to what it would be in real life, by analyzing video recordings of actual matches.  With only a limited amount of information, our method is able to accurately predict the outcomes of these scenarios, resulting in an increase of 15\% in wins over the standard agent.

Understanding seismic data involves inverse modeling to expand the dataset, which is a complex task that has been challenging to achieve with computational power. Waveform inversion is a renowned method for forwarding seismic data but has limitations when it comes to expanding datasets. Source waveform inversion has been successful in scaling data sets but has restrictions in timing information. This research aims to combine the advantages of both methods by introducing expanded source time-domain waveform inversion, which expands datasets in time domains while maintaining the efficiency of source waveform inversion. This will be achieved by developing a nonlinear operator that represents expanding time domains, and we will demonstrate this method on synthetic data generated by elastic equations.

To analyze the dynamics of a species competition model that accounts for colonization and extinction events, we developed a voter model with uncertainty, inspired by the James-Stein estimator to simulate species elimination and species coexistence. This model includes parameters for the strength of species competition, the rate of colonization, and the rate of extinction, which can vary between species. We studied the species competition model in both a random grid environment and a grid environment with periodic boundary conditions. Our results show that a state of coexistence or species elimination can occur, influenced by the rate of colonization and the distance between species competition and species elimination. To identify these conditions, we established upper and lower bounds on the difference between species competition and species elimination in the random grid setting. When the rate of colonization is greater than the square root of the rate of species elimination, a state of coexistence can occur. Conversely, when the rate of colonization is less than the negative square root of the rate of species elimination, species elimination occurs. Similarly, in the periodic grid setting, we found the conditions under which species elimination or coexistence occur.

An integrated data and power networking system is proposed, allowing for the coexistence of D2D transmissions. This integrated approach leverages a intellect reflecting surface to achieve optimal power distribution and maximized D2D transmission capacity. The problem is combinatorial in nature and a polynomial-time algorithm is developed to find an approximate optimal solution. Simulation results demonstrate the proposed scheme's effectiveness in maximizing D2D transmission capacity and reducing power waste. The integrated data and power networking approach can support up to 70% more D2D transmissions compared to a separate power and data networking system, and improves power utilization ratio by approximately 25%.

A flow field can be complex, varying across both x and y dimensions, yet many situations involving fluid dynamics only require knowledge of flow characteristics along a single line, particularly across y dimensions at a fixed x point. In such cases, having a precise control over hot wire anemometry in real-time would provide significant practical benefits. Real-time control could minimize noise generated by the anemometry system, ensure an optimal angle of incidence for better sample accuracy, and prevent the anemometry wire from becoming clogged or damaged by debris. This study presents a novel distant control method for a single-point LDV system that enables two-dimensional measurements. By utilizing a optical delay line and a photomultiplier tube, we implemented a distant control system where the signal processing unit is separated from the anemometry head. As a result, we minimized noise generated by electrical components, ensured accurate measurements at an optimal angle of incidence, and protected the anemometry wire from damage. This distant control system also allows for a much simpler design of an optical fiber LDV system.

The issue of astigmatization in Transmission Electron Microscopy (TEM) images poses an ongoing challenge, causing difficulties in identifying specific structures and positioning molecules accurately. Since the shape of astigmatism influences the focus of an image, accurately determining its form is crucial for correcting it. We propose a method that involves finding the exact shape of astigmatism by capturing a phase plate's uncorrected image, which has a known and programmable shape. By multiplying the uncorrected image by its complex conjugate, we can determine the form of astigmatism and therefore correct it. Using both theoretical and experimental approaches, we found that a phase plate with a parabolic shape can correct astigmatism and improve the resolution of the TEM image. Furthermore, we found that a disk with a specific phase pattern can direct the electron beam to a particular location on the sample, allowing for the correction of astigmatism and increasing the resolution of the TEM image.

We provide explicit definitions for the spectral and orbital stability of solitary waves in a model that combines the Klein-Gordon equation and an anharmonic oscillator. We also conduct a comprehensive analysis of the linearized equation's spectrum at the solitary wave state.

We derive a modified version of the classical Leopoldt theorem for non-commutative Lie algebras over Q, incorporating a notion of reducedness for elements within its associated Poincaré-Birkhoff-Witt algebra. Additionally, we establish that the image of its I-function corresponds to the interior of a specific compact convex polytope defined by moment conditions, essentially mirroring the geometric interpretation of the classical Leopoldt theorem.

In experiments involving particle collisions, identifying neutral long-lived particles relies on either finding decay products at unusual locations or missing energy. The choice between these methods depends on the particle's properties, as well as those of the detector used. To better understand the effectiveness of these methods, we are examining how they complement each other, with a focus on the Belle II experiment and axion-like particles produced through the decay of certain mesons. A new detection approach for these particles, which involve a two-body decay process where a meson transforms into another particle and then a form of missing energy, has been proposed. This strategy, using data from Belle II equivalent to $50$ times its current amount, should allow the experiment to discover particles of a very low mass that leave little trace, with certain characteristics that include a minimum production probability and a minimum time that the particle remains active. This detection method is anticipated to significantly improve the discovery potential of Belle II for these types of particles by as much as two orders of magnitude. The most efficient way of detecting these particles, which could weigh a few hundred million times less than an electron, would involve searching for decay products at unusual locations and analyzing energy data from various experiments involving the collision of high-speed particles, which include those carried out in experiments involving the Belle II experiment and a different experiment in which particles collide with stationary particles in the form of a metal target.
